why: It says the street had formed by the Ming as a patrol road along the wall, called the West Horse Road, which is the one page read that names the wall-side street's use. It is a stub about one street of one town, whose only reference is a 1992 place-name gazetteer of Tong county (北京市通县地名志, p. 32), not a record from the period; it gives no width and no date closer than "the Ming", and it does not say whether building on the road was barred.

It gives the wall-side streets on all four sides inside the outer wall, 20 to 25 m wide, which is both the one measured patrol road read and the evidence that Chang'an's wards stood back from the rampart. Its note numbers point to a reference list the page does not print, and it contradicts itself on some counts (108, 109 or 110 wards; 8 or 11 north-south avenues; a perimeter of 35.5 or 36.7 km). The 20-25 m wall-side street figure is the same in all three places it appears. The measurement goes back to the excavators' own report (唐代长安城考古纪略, 《考古》 1963), which would be the closer source if it can be read. It describes a capital planned on a grid in the 580s, not of a provincial seat, and it does not describe what stood on the wall-side street.

It states the Tang foot as 30.7 cm, the figure the authors check a Tang ruler from Shanzhou against; that ruler is 15.2 cm, unevenly graduated, and a half-foot only by the authors' own reading, so it gives a foot of about 30.4 cm and does not itself establish the 30.7, which the article asserts without a source, and the article does not say that the Tang kept a large and a small foot, 30.7 cm being the large. It gives the pace as eight feet under the Zhou, six under the Qin, and five builder's feet (yingzao chi, the Ming and Qing builder's foot of about 31 to 32 cm) in the old reckoning, which turns paces into meters; the five-foot pace is therefore stated for the late imperial reckoning, not for the Tang or the Song, and holds for them only on other evidence. A foot's length varied from dynasty to dynasty.

It places the foot soldiers' guard house, with its jail, across from the main guard house, which is the arrangement a map's two gate stations follow. It is a visitor's account, on a travel blog that carries affiliate advertising, of the reconstruction completed in 2007. It describes one barrier, a shogunate checkpoint on a highway rather than the gate of a walled town, so a town gate's two stations borrow its arrangement rather than being shown by it. The reconstruction shows the barrier as the records of its late-Edo repair describe it; that it is faithful rests here on the blogger's own statement, and the town's site on the reconstruction (hakonesekisyo.jp) is the closer source.

It says the barrier was rebuilt in 2007 from the detailed records of its large repair at the end of the Edo period, which is what lets the rebuilt plan stand for the historical one, and that the main guard house was where travelers were examined. It gives no plan, no measurements and no account of where each building stands.

It is the one page read that measures the moats of several cities side by side - Qufu, Kaifeng, Xi'an, Jingzhou, Xiangyang and Guide - and it counts the enemy platforms of Yuci and Guide. It is a compilation marked as taken from the internet with no author and no sources, some of its figures disagree with other pages (Xi'an's moat, 20 by 10 m against 18 by 6 m elsewhere; Pingyao's towers every 60 m against 50 m). Two of its six moats are outliers, not the ordinary city moat: the page itself calls Xiangyang's 130-250 m moat rare in the whole country, and Guide's runs from 25 to 500 m wide, more lake than ditch; they bound the broad end of the range only. Kaifeng's 16.66 by 3.33 m and Qufu's 3.3 m read as round old measures (5 zhang by 1 zhang, and 1 zhang) converted at the modern one-third-meter chi, so a few percent larger than the Ming-Qing measure they came from.
It states the doctrine behind a castle's two gates, which is why our castle draws a front and a rear gate.

It gives the gate's working: a large central gate, 2.5 ken wide, as the way from one block to the next, left open by day and shut at 10 pm or in an emergency to cut off traffic, with wickets to either side, and the gates at both ends of a block shut at night. These are signed encyclopedia entries that cite no ordinance: the Nipponica's is by Inagaki Shisei, a period-drama consultant and novelist rather than a historian, who points to the late-Edo Morisada Mankō, and the Heibonsha's is by Yoshiwara Ken'ichirō; the 10 pm is a modern reading of the Edo hour yotsu, which shifted with the season. The Nipponica entry speaks of Edo, Kyoto, Osaka and similar cities, so the 2.5 ken is a great city's gate and no provincial town's gate is measured; and the older Heibonsha entry for kido on the same page puts an Edo gate's posts about 2 ken apart, so these accounts give the opening as 2 to 2.5 ken, not one fixed width.

It sets out the upper levels of the Ming and Qing military examination - provincial, metropolitan and palace - and places the Qing palace examination in the Hall of Supreme Harmony before the emperor, which puts those levels at the provincial and imperial capitals. It does not itself say where the provincial examination sat; its Ming palace level is thin (its own list of Ming top military graduates names one man, Wang Laipin); and it omits the stage below, the county, prefectural and qualifying examinations a Qing military candidate passed to become a military licentiate, the first of them held at the county seat - so it cannot show that the county seat had no part in the military examination. It says nothing of where candidates trained or whether a county seat had private martial schools.

It says the range stood at the front of a samurai residence and housed retainers and menservants, that its roof ran on unbroken from the range, that a samurai gate had a guard room projecting at each side with its form fixed by the house's rank, and that one surviving domain gate once ran to a 120 m frontage. They give no range's depth or height, and the rank rules they mention are the daimyo's and the shogun's direct retainers' in general, not any one domain's. The 120 m frontage is a daimyo house's gate, the largest scale of samurai residence, and cannot size a lesser retainer's gate.

Its general sentence says the nagayamon was one form of an early-modern samurai residence's front gate and also served as a storeroom and as servants' quarters. The gate it describes is not historical evidence: it was probably built in the Taisho period (1912-1926), and the page says no Edo-period gate range survives in the old castle town; only the general sentence is used. That sentence is the city's own one-line summary on a visitor page, with no references and it cannot say how common each use was. It describes a samurai residence's gate, so applying it to a government compound's gate carries the form over to another kind of building.

It gives the sizes and shapes of real town blocks - Heian-kyo's 40-jo square, Edo's 60-ken square with its open core (measured in the longer Kyoto ken, which the entry gives as 39 jo, about 118 m, not 60 of the later 1.82 m ken), and the rectangular block most castle towns used - which is what a drawn city's grid is measured against. It describes Japanese planned towns rather than the Chinese walled seats our cities also draw on, and its sizes are the planned units, not surveys of any one town as built.

It describes the block, the shop frontage and the back alley of an Edo commoner quarter in one place, which is the fabric our city maps pack. It speaks of Ginza only, one district of the shogun's capital, which is a larger and more regular place than the provincial city we draw. It measures in the longer Kyoto ken, by which it puts its 60 ken at about 120 m, not in the shorter Edo ken. Its three-to-five-ken shop frontage comes in a passage asking the reader to picture the old lots from today's street, where it says the same frontage still holds, so it is the column's picture and not a dated Edo measurement. It also says the lots' interiors changed after 1657 without saying how, and that what the open ground at the block's center was used for is not known.

It attests the rice stock kept inside a castle against siege, one of the two granaries our capital draws. The article carries a notice that it shows no verifiable references, and the siege-store claim rests on it alone.

It places the cheap inn at the edge of the post town and prices it against the inn with meals, which is what decides where a map puts its cheapest lodging. It speaks of the Tokaido's post-stations, not of a provincial seat. Its five-times price is a late-Edo figure, from after the inn with meals had spread; the page itself says the firewood-fee inn was the usual lodging before the Edo period, so the ratio does not carry to earlier eras. And it puts the cheap inns at the edge of the post town "and such places" (はずれなど), which is where they usually stood, not a rule.

It places the cheapest lodging in one small district of a Chinese city and says that everyone who slept there was poor, which is what places a cheap lodging house inside a city's walls on a map. It dates the capital's grand hotels and temple lodgings but gives no date for the chicken-feather inns, which it lists among the lodgings found "since the Republic" (民国以来, after 1912), so what it says of them may describe early-twentieth-century Beijing rather than the imperial city; it concerns the imperial capital rather than a county seat, and it gives no count of the cheap inns.

It repeats the local saying for the streets and lanes of a surviving Ming and Qing walled seat, the kind of city our county seats are modeled on, against the number of house compounds they serve. "Four main streets, eight small streets and seventy-two lanes" is the town's traditional saying, not a count: seventy-two is a conventional number, and other accounts give eighty-four streets and lanes, or hundreds if dead ends and newer streets are included. The 4,000 compounds and the population are both counted today, not in the Ming or Qing; and it gives the streets' count, not their width or the share of the ground they take.

It places one named Ming official's private garden, built after he was dismissed from office, just outside a city gate, which is the near-city retreat this record asks about. It is one garden, in Suzhou, the richest garden city of late imperial China; it says the garden was his but not whether he lived there or in town, gives no distance from the wall, and says nothing about how common such a garden was. The garden whose size and layout it describes (20,390 m² in its infobox, "over 30,000 m², 50 mu" in its text) is the Qing rebuilding of 1798 and the enlargement of 1873-76, made on the site of a Ming garden that had fallen into ruin, so only the garden's founding and its place outside the gate are Ming.

It gives the one measured extent found for a place named a guanxiang: about 350 m by 50 m, a single street of shop-houses. Its limits are large: Xiashi is a Jiangnan market town, not a walled administrative seat, and the guanxiang it is named for was a checkpoint on a water and land route, not a gate suburb; the extent is today's protected district, bounded on the west by a modern road (Renmin Road) and on the east by the Luotang River, so its 50 m is the strip of street and the lots behind it back to the river, not the width of a street, and the article cites no source for the figure; the buildings standing in it are mostly Qing to Republican, restored by the city government in 2008-2012.

It says the channel was drawn in the Ueda domain's Sengoku-family era from Amagafuchi, at the foot of the castle town, to irrigate three villages downstream (Suwabe, Akiwa and Kami-Shiojiri) - river water taken in at the foot of a castle and put to the fields below the town. It also says the channel carries the urban area's rainwater, a role it calls one no other weir has. It names no documents; the rainwater role belongs to the channel as it runs through the modern city today, beside the page's account of urban development and household wastewater, and is no evidence that the Edo-period channel drained the castle town; its intake has since moved upstream (to Hori, then Komaki), and its present course runs in a tunnel under the river and beneath a shopping street; the page itself is unsure when the channel took the name Masuami (probably before 1882); it gives no date beyond the era; and it does not say the channel was drawn from the castle moat itself.

It gives a counted ward at a castle-town entrance on a trunk road: made in the early Edo period when the highway was re-routed, lined with lodging inns for villagers on official business and with tea shops, and holding 124 houses in the early 1830s. Odawara was also a post town, which swelled its roadside trade; the count is of houses, not shops; the leaflet does not say whether the ward lay inside or outside the town's outer enclosure; for this ward it names the domain lord's 1645 diary for the ward's first mention but does not name the record behind the 124-house count, which is also about two centuries later than the ward's founding; and the PDF is an image with no text layer, so its words can be read but not searched.

It gives the one head count found of a domain's retainers split between the castle town and the countryside: 1,015 castle-town samurai against 8,202 rural samurai in 1639. It names no primary source for the figures; it does not say whether the 1,015 includes the upper retainers its koku average leaves out, and it says the two names came into use only in the late eighteenth century. Satsuma is the extreme case of a domain that kept its retainers on the land, so the split describes one unusual domain, not the Edo-period norm. And it is a split across the whole domain, not around one town: the 8,202 rural samurai lived in 113 outer districts spread over the domain, each its own small garrison settlement of about seventy on average. So it gives the castle town's share of a domain's retainers, not how a city's samurai were divided between the town and its own surroundings.

A public museum states in two sentences that Satsuma set up 113 outer districts besides the Kagoshima castle town, settled warriors in them and had them farm in peacetime. Its one number, the 113, comes with no date and no source, so it cannot say when in the period that count held. The page gives no count of warriors or of households. It also describes Satsuma alone, a domain whose arrangement was unusual.

It says that the apprentice lived in the shop he served from about the age of ten, which is why a town's merchant servants are not drawn as houses of their own. It is written of the merchant houses of the great cities as much as of a county town's, and it says nothing of the building beyond that the apprentice lived in it.

It states the textbook layout, that windbreak belts are laid in parallel at right angles to a wind from one fixed direction, which is the bearing the towns page tests the drawn belts against; the same page says that where winds come from several directions the belts are laid in a checkerboard instead, so the right-angle rule holds only against a single prevailing wind. Its example is the American-type belts planted in Hokkaido in the modern period rather than the homestead groves of older Japan; the layout is the physics of a wind wall, not a record of how pre-modern farmers planted.

It gives, from an official research body, the layout of the main windbreak against the prevailing wind and the secondary belts set mostly at right angles to it. It is orchard practice, written for windbreak installations in general and laid out across an orchard's blocks rather than around a settlement. It is not a description of how pre-modern farmsteads or villages were sheltered: it carries the physical principle, not evidence that any period village was laid out this way.

They agree that the surcharge paid for the shogunal intendants' offices until 1725, when the shogunate took it and paid the offices' costs itself. They disagree on why: the one signed entry (Oguchi Yujiro's, in the Sekai Dai-hyakka Jiten) blames the intendants' misuse of public money; the unsigned Mypedia entry says, in a single sentence, that the costs ran below the surcharge; the others give no reason, and none gives a figure for any office's costs. The 1725 order itself, which the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten names from the Tokugawa Kinreiko, has not been read here. It concerns the shogunate's own intendancies, not a daimyo's county offices.
It attests the corner turret as a standard element, one of the three things this page says make a castle read as one.

It places a large bridge on the main way in and out of Pan Gate, near the gate tower. The page gives that nearness only as a scenic grouping with the tower and the Ruiguang Pagoda, not as a measured position. It never mentions a water gate, so the fact that Pan Gate pairs a land gate with a water gate, and so the bridge's adjacency to that water gate, has to come from another source. It dates the first bridge only to the Northern Song and the standing one to an 1872 rebuilding, so the present span, 66 m long and about 10 m high, is a late Qing structure and not evidence for an earlier bridge's size. It describes a bridge outside the wall over the moat-canal, and says nothing about roads or bridges inside the wall.

It shows a city canal cut straight off a river at its own mouth, dug by a townsman rather than as part of a defense, which is the second of the two forms a river city's cargo canal takes. Its history rests on one general reference, the 1983 Kadokawa place-name dictionary of Osaka, with no inline citation for the 1600 date or the digger. It says where the canal branched off the Tosabori but not what its mouth looked like; Osaka was an unwalled commercial castle town on a delta laced with rivers, so it says nothing about how a walled city's canal met a moat, and a canal that no longer exists is described from records rather than as seen.

It shows a canal that was also a castle's outer moat opening straight off a river, and counts the bridges over a city canal of about 3 km. It was a moat only from 1585 to 1615: it was filled under the peace that ended the Winter Campaign, re-dug after the castle fell, and was a town canal through the Edo period, so it shows a canal's mouth on a river rather than a lasting moat's. Its list of fourteen bridges is of today's crossings and does not say which stood in the Edo period, so it bounds rather than gives a period density; and Osaka was an unwalled castle town, not a walled Chinese city.

It puts the pond's everyday uses - washing, laundry, fish, water against fire, irrigation - and its other names in one readable place, each attributed to the work it came from, and it says plainly that the origin of the half shape lacks the sources to settle it. Its limits: its examples are Taiwan's, mostly of the Qing and later, so it speaks for south-Chinese settler practice and not for the mainland or an older period; its uses are the pond's possible uses, not a count of how often each was made; some of what it relays is twentieth-century living memory, not premodern practice (the Pingtung Guangyu hall's fish include tilapia, brought to Taiwan in 1946), and its illustration is AI-generated; and the works it relays are themselves public (the folk-artifact dictionary at dict.th.gov.tw, the Hakka center's 半月池 page, the National Cultural Memory Bank's entry), so a claim that matters is better taken from them.

It is the one readable page found that states the meaning given to the half circle - a half-full moon, because a full moon wanes - and names the Hakka enclosed house's front pond among its examples. Its limits are severe: it is an anonymous text, carries no references and no date for the belief, has visible typos. Its advice is written for modern self-built and luxury houses and gives the same rule for fountains and swimming pools, and it comes from a furniture-trade media account, not from anyone who studies vernacular building; it shows that the reading is current, not that the ponds were dug for it.

It says in plain words where the trees of a shrine or temple stand: single sacred trees in front of the buildings or along the approach, and a small grove behind the main building and around its sides, often a remnant of the old forest; and that the groves at the tiniest local shrines and temples hold only several to a dozen or so trees each. Its limits are that it speaks of shrines and temples together and of today, not of the Edo period; that it gives no counts or measurements; and that its placement of the grove is a general statement whose named examples are all great shrines (Shimogamo, Omiwa, Togakushi, Ise, Kasuga). It never says where the few trees of a tiny local shrine stand, so the behind-and-sides layout at a village shrine is our reading of it, not something it shows at that scale.

It is the one survey read that sorts shrine groves by which sides of the hall they stand on, and it names the forms: a grove behind the hall, behind and at the sides, at the sides only, and - on a hill-shaped rise - all around it; and it ties each to where the hall sits on its slope. Its limits are that its named examples (Hie, Nezu, Kanda, Atago) are great city shrines, not a village's tutelary shrine; that it sorts the groves that survived, not the groves that were planted - the paper itself says many of these groves burned in the war and were replanted after it, and that the grounds have shrunk and been built on (halls, fire stores, parks), so a grove at the sides only may be what the city left rather than a form anyone chose; that its population is small (27 slope-sited shrines with groves, of 122 listed); that it never states what its percentages are shares of, and they do not come out as whole counts of 27, so they give the forms' order of commonness and are not used as rates; and that its English summary glosses the figures differently from its Japanese text, which is the one cited.

It dates to 1728 a reclamation laid out with supply canals along the edge of the former reservoir and a drain down its center, which is the separated layout in an Edo-period work. It describes one large shogunal project on the Kanto plain rather than a village's own ditches, and it says nothing of how the plots inside were fed.

It says the older Kanto-school water use made one channel serve both supply and drainage, and that the Kishu school separated the drainage rivers, which dates the separated layout's arrival on the Kanto plain to the 1720s and the combined one there to before it; the techniques were Izawa's own, brought from Kishu, so the page does not say separation was new everywhere in 1722, nor that the combined layout ended where the Kishu school did not reach. It is written about the large alluvial plains of eastern Japan, and it describes trunk canals and drainage rivers, not the ditches between one village's plots.

It names the separation of supply from drainage as a feature of Izawa's method and says that at Konuma the drainage was gathered down the center, so that the villages below kept their water, which is a second dated Edo case of the separated layout. It describes a reclaimed marsh, not an old village's fields. The layout it gives is the trunk layout of a whole reclamation ordered by the shogunate: supply brought in from the Minuma canal's western branch, one drain down the former marsh's center, and the new fields divided among nine villages. It does not describe the ditches of single fields. It presents the separation of supply from drainage as the method of the Kishu school, brought in during the 1720s, and sets it against the older Kanto school's river dams, retention ponds and flood basins. So it dates the separated layout in planned reclamation from that time, not in the fields of villages settled long before.

It records that Edo-period weirs were classed by their angle to the river's main flow, and that the oblique minote weir, following the flow, put its intake on the side toward which the water ran; it also says oblique weirs were common before the Meiji period. It gives no angle in degrees, neither for the weir nor for the canal leaving at its intake.

The Tedori fan is a Japanese fan under paddy, the landform the record's comb fans depict, and its abstract shows the water standing on the paddies recharging the mid-fan's groundwater beside the river's water. It also measures a disturbed state: after a 2015 headwater landslide, with the river's flow down, when the paddy water's share of the recharge rose because the river's fell. So it is cited for the physical process only (paddy water recharges the fan's groundwater), not for any share or amount, nor for any premodern practice, and only its abstract is cited.

It shows that an Edo land survey reckoned a paddy bund at one shaku (about 30 cm), a premodern figure for the bund's width. It is a survey convention for tax, not a measurement of real bunds, and the survey took out more than the bund: a one-shaku strip beside it on each side as well, so one shaku is the bund's reckoned width, not the width of the whole deduction (about three shaku across a bund line). The quoted order of 1726 reckons each holding's deduction at one shaku five sun, which reads as its one-shaku edge strip plus half the shared one-shaku bund, consistent with the definition. The figure rests on the order it quotes. It is about Japan only.

It gives two Edo-period dimensions: the intake, a wooden trough about 2 ken (3.6 m) wide and 24 ken long, and the new channel cut below the split from the Hoshi River, about 6 ken wide. That is one of the great shogunal canals, watering a whole plain, so it marks the top of the main-canal band rather than a village's main; the passage giving both widths carries no footnote, so the article's own references do not stand behind these figures; it also does not say whether the 6 ken is measured at the bed, the water surface or the bank-top.

It sums up the excavated paddies as divided by bunds and channels, with intakes and outlets fitted with weirs and structures for regulating the amount of water, found from the Late Jomon onward, a basic form it says was handed down to the present, so the bund, the channel and the inlet are all premodern forms. Its "reinforced with sheet boards and stakes" is not true of every site (the Hattori and early Sena paddies were not). Its only sizes are for plots (the Kofun-period Mifuro plots of 3-5 m², about one or two tatami); it gives none for a bund, a channel or an intake. The paddies it describes are Jomon to Kofun, far earlier than the Edo and imperial Chinese eras the setting is modeled on, and that the form lasted is the page's own claim.

It states that each square of the grid was planned to adjoin a road and a waterway (考えられている: the system's design, not a survey of squares found), and that in basins such as Omi the grid's axes ran with the main slope toward Lake Biwa and at right angles to it. So it carries a right-angled layout of channels on Japanese plains of the ancient and medieval periods, peaking about the ninth century, though that layout is this record's reading: the page never says the channels themselves ran at right angles. It is a general history citing no excavation for these sentences; it hedges the ninth-century peak as what is thought; and it describes land division at the scale of the 109 m square, not the ditches inside one. It says that outside the Yamato and Yamashiro core the grid lost its continuity and turned off true north-south. It says the grid was laid out in units of about 100 cho (about 120 ha) whose lines do not meet from one unit to the next (the Nobi plain). And it says that where floods, volcanic eruptions or large, shifting rivers struck, the grid itself did not take hold and vanished.

It is an excavator's own account that Heian paddies were laid out inside large bunds and waterways whose large bunds faced east-west and north-south, so the right-angled frame is a dug and dated fact at one place, not only a land-register idea. It shows one site; the relation to the jori system is given as the accepted view, not proved; and it says the small plots inside the frame were often out of shape and did not follow the grid in detail. It gives a direction for the large bunds only, not for the waterways, and no distance between the large bunds (only the small plots' sides, 5 to 20 m). So it cannot show that the frame kept the jori's 1-cho (about 109 m) interval, or that the channels themselves ran at right angles.

It gives the length of the Chinese foot from the Qin to the Three Kingdoms, and says the Warring States foot was essentially the same, so a width given in chi in a classical text can be put in inches. It does not say which foot any given text used: before the Qin standardized measures in 221 BC each state kept its own, and the Kaogongji has been argued to use a Qi foot (Wen Renjun, Kaogu 1983), so its widths in inches assume that foot matched this one. Its Qin-to-Three-Kingdoms range rests on one companion to a Han mathematical classic (Shen, Crossley and Lun, 1999) and its Warring States sentence on a translation of Sima Qian, neither read here; it calls the figure what researchers surmise; and the range is how the foot varied over five centuries, not a single value.

It states that an Edo new-field village laid out its roads, fields and house plots on a plan, so its form was regular, and that the street villages common on the Kanto plain set each house's land behind it in strips of equal area - the premodern evidence for an evenly divided planned reclamation. It gives no geometry beyond the strips and says nothing of a grid of paddies. Its strip villages are on the Kanto uplands (Musashino, a diluvial plateau watered by common wells and branches off the aqueducts), which was dry-field land, not paddy. In Heibonsha, the reclaimed new fields where paddy was made took another form: houses in a line along the dike, with each household's fields near the house and fairly compact; Heibonsha adds that the common form was the clustered village with scattered holdings, and that new fields added onto an old village's land founded no new settlement, so the planned layout is one form among several.

It describes a planned Edo reclamation's layout: houses in a row along a road, a long narrow strip of field and woodland behind each, fields allotted nearly equally in many villages at the start, and, in the plateau's south, the rows running the way of the canals dug along the highways (in the north, watered by deep wells, the page says the rows run in a comparatively free direction). Its limits: the land is dry field and woodland on a waterless plateau, not paddy, so it shows an Edo planned layout but not a paddy one, and the canals the rows follow were dug first for drinking water, not to irrigate paddy; the "checkerboard" in its section title is the series' heading, not a claim about these villages.

It ties the street's name and course to the funerary ground at its head, which is how this page locates Rendaino. The article gives two competing origins for the name, and the one this page uses carries no citation and no date while the other does.

It dates the Ikeda domain's reclamation of the bay chiefly to the Kanbun era (1661-72), with other domains' projects carrying the pre-Meiji reclamation to about 6,800 ha and the Fujita works following from 1899, and Kojo village's to the very end of the early modern period, and says Kojo's subdivided fields were consolidated into blocks by readjustment under its upper farmers - the evidence that the blocks there are a later work, not the Edo layout. It gives no date for that consolidation (its context places it before the war, alongside the mechanization of the 1920s-30s) and does not describe the Edo-period plots or say how they came to be subdivided.

It is the study of where the rack stood and why, read from distribution maps: a technique born in the Kinki (a record of 841) that spread outward, taken up readily where harvests were rainy or paddies wet and slowly where autumns were sunny, its tall form following deep snow. Its limits: it maps the practice of the 1880s to the 1950s, after rack drying had spread for two centuries, and it reads the map at the scale of regions, noting that the forms mix locally. Its thesis is diffusion, so whether a region had racks also turned on its distance from the Kinki and on local resistance (Kyushu still dried on the ground in 1881), not on weather alone. The racks gathered by the house rest on one sentence about the changeable San'in coast, with no count, whose stated reason is threshing in the yard; the paper does not say that racks stood away from the house where the weather was settled - its one such example is a Sanyo town building a rack in each field - so that half of our rule is our inference.
It places the ground at the head of the road that became Senbon-dōri, corroborating the Wikipedia article on the street.

It is a primary text from well before the setting's period describing dry grain sown in lines in furrows between ridges, which is the texture the maps draw on a dry plot. It describes a method one official, Zhao Guo, promoted from the capital in the first century BCE, calling its dimensions an ancient method; it says the farmers of the capital commanderies around Chang'an, Hedong, Hongnong and the frontier towns took it up, but that is the state's own account of its own program, with no count of fields, it does not say whether the method lasted past the Han.

It is a primary text from before the setting's period showing grain sown with drills in rows and thinned to a set spacing, which grounds the rows the maps draw on a dry plot. It describes North China's dry farming in the sixth century, largely from the Yellow River plain; the drill (耬) is named only in the author's notes (on a quoted Han memorial, and in the seed chapter), though his main text has the ox walk slowly so the seed falls evenly while the sower treads the row bottom. The spacing is "one stand (科) to the chi" and for good land only: a stand may be more than one stalk, a Han author he quotes has poor land sown thinner, and his chi is the Northern Wei measure of about 28 to 30 cm, near but not the same as a foot or the Japanese shaku.

It gives the hours in plain numbers - about 6 or more for sun crops, about 3 to 4 for half-shade crops, 1 to 2 for shade crops - and puts daikon, eggplant, cucumber and the beans among the first, turnip, komatsuna, taro, negi and ginger among the second, mitsuba, shiso and myoga among the third. Its limits are that it is a modern seed company's advice for modern cultivars, not an Edo farm manual; that its hours are round figures for good growth, not a measured threshold below which a crop fails; that it does not say which season the hours are counted in; and that only its sun class is a firm threshold - it says half-shade crops also grow under dappled light all day, so their 3 to 4 hours of direct sun is not a minimum. The page is in Shift_JIS, an older Japanese text encoding, and reads correctly only when decoded as such.
It places the crossroads on the way to Toribeno, the siting this page uses; the temple's own article beside it carries the same.

It says where a samurai residence's vegetable field lay: the woods, bamboo and garden south of the pond (a waterway runs east-west through about the middle of the grounds) were used as a field in the Edo period, and the grounds once fed the household. That is a working plot in the southern part of the grounds, in the zone the formal garden now holds; the page does not say where the house stood relative to it. Its limits are that it is one house, of one domain's retainers, not an official compound; that it gives no size and no date within the period; that it describes the ground as it was used, not a plan of beds; and that it states the Edo-period use without its evidence, about grounds that have been restored and landscaped since.
